title: Puzzle Page Mini Grid
story: A weekend newspaper runs a mini number puzzle: a 6 × 6 grid split into six boxes of 2 rows by 3 columns. Readers fill each empty square with a digit from 1 to 6 so every row, column and box holds each digit exactly once.
The editor wants a program that fills in a grid before it is printed. The program must also catch broken puzzles, because a typo in the clues can make a grid impossible to complete.
task: Write solvePuzzle(grid). grid is a list of 6 strings of length 6. Each character is a digit '1' to '6' (a printed clue) or '.' (an empty square). The boxes are rows 0–1, 2–3 and 4–5, each split into columns 0–2 and 3–5. Square (r, c) is in box ⌊r/2⌋ × 2 + ⌊c/3⌋.

Return the completed grid as 6 strings of digits, keeping every clue where it is. If the puzzle has several solutions, return any one. If it has none, including when the clues themselves repeat a digit in a row, column or box, return an empty list.
constraints: grid has 6 rows, each a string of 6 characters from '1'–'6' and '.'.
Any valid completed grid is accepted.

examples.explanation: Row 0 needs a 6. The top-right box already has a 6 at row 1, column 4, so the 6 in row 0 must go in the top-left box, and the only empty square there in row 0 is column 0. Reasoning like this, or trial and error, fills in the rest, and this puzzle has exactly one solution.
The top-left square's row already contains 2 and 3, its column contains 4 and 5, and its box contains 6 and 1. No digit is left for that square.

hints: Pick any empty square and list the digits it could take. What should happen when that list is empty?

Fill the empty squares one at a time, trying each digit not already in that square's row, column or box. If a later square has no digit left, an earlier choice was wrong: go back and try the next digit there.

Keep three lists of sets (or boolean tables) holding the digits used in each row, column and box. Then the question "can digit d go at (r, c)?" takes three lookups. Fill the sets from the clues first, and if a clue repeats a digit, return [] at once.

Collect the empty squares in a list. fill(i) returns true when all squares from position i onward are filled. For each allowed digit at square i, place it and mark the three sets. If fill(i + 1) succeeds, return true at once without undoing anything. Otherwise clear the square and unmark the sets, and return false when no digit works.
bruteForce: Try every combination of digits in the empty squares and check the full grid each time. With 24 empty squares that is 624, about 4.7 × 1018 grids, which would take well over a century at a billion grids per second.
The opposite shortcut is to take the first digit that fits and never go back. It is fast but often gets stuck, because an early guess that looks fine can leave a later square with no digit.

walkthrough: Fill squares in reading order, trying only digits that do not clash with the square's row, column or box. If a square has no digit left, undo the most recent choice and try its next digit. This approach is called backtracking.

• For square (0, 0), the box already has 1, 2 and 3, so try 4. Square (0, 3) can then only be 1, and (0, 4) can only be 5. Square (0, 5) needs the last digit, 6, but the top-right box already has a 6. This is a dead end, so undo back to (0, 0).

• Try 5 at (0, 0). Now (0, 3) can be 1 or 4. With 1, square (0, 4) must be 4 and (0, 5) again needs 6, which is a dead end. With 4, square (0, 4) has no digit at all, which is also a dead end. Undo back to (0, 0).
• Try 6 at (0, 0), as the example's reasoning predicted. The search then continues into the next rows.

Two details matter. When fill(i + 1) succeeds, return at once without undoing, or the solved grid gets erased on the way back up. The clues must also be loaded into the sets before the search starts, so that a grid with a repeated clue is rejected instead of being "solved".
solution.timeWhy: A worst-case bound for e empty squares with up to 6 digits each. The row, column and box checks reject most digits immediately, so each test puzzle here needs at most a few hundred placements.
solution.spaceWhy: The list of empty squares and a recursion depth of e, plus fixed-size sets for rows, columns and boxes.
solution.takeaway: Constraint puzzles follow one template. Keep a set of used values for every rule, choose a value for the next open slot only if all the sets allow it, recurse, and undo the choice on failure. Stop at the first success, and validate the starting state before you search.
